newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope hailed in Lebanon, urges end to divisions.
newsitem.headline: Pope hailed in Lebanon, urges end to divisions.

text.p: Pope John Paul, given a tumultuous welcome in Lebanon, called on its people on Saturday to break down the barriers of mistrust erected by civil war and build a society open to Christians and Moslems alike.

"Do not build new walls in the bosom of your country," the Pope told more than 15,000 young Lebanese who thronged to the hilltop shrine of Harissa, north of Beirut, for the first public event of his 32-hour visit -- his first to the Middle East.

"Your task is to build bridges between people, between families and between the different communities," the Pope told the youths, who gave him one of the warmest receptions he has had from a crowd on foreign trips in recent years.

"You must also ensure that each Lebanese, especially the young, may take part in the life of society, in the common home," the 76-year-old Pope said, adding that gestures of reconciliation would allow "trust to replace mistrust".
The boisterous, flag-waving youths, who included about 500 invited Moslems, repeatedly broke into his speech with calls of "Long Live Peace" and "John Paul Two, We Love You".

The chants changed to "Freedom, Freedom" when Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, the Maronite patriarch and head of the Lebanese Church, gave an address demanding democracy, equal rights and justice for young Lebanese.
The Pope is known to regard Lebanon as an example for a region where Christian communities are in decline.

But many of Lebanon's minority Christians complain that they have been marginalised from politics since the 1975-1990 civil war, from which they emerged defeated. Others refuse to participate because they believe the pro-Syrian government will not give them a fair deal.

The concerns were highlighted by a speaker at the service, student Pierre Najm, who told the Pope that many young people had lost faith in politics, religion and their country amid a loss of fundamental freedoms.

"We ask you, you who have come here to sow hope, to dare to say out loud the things which we are afraid to say and which we have lost the habit of expressing. Be our courage and call things by their name," Najm said.
The youths virtually mobbed the frail Pope when he arrived at Harissa, a shrine to the Virgin Mary overlooking the sea.

As the Pope gazed down from a balcony on thousands of the youths who filled a square outside the basilicia, they cheered and clapped in scenes more familiar to a rock concert than a religious ceremony and sang him "Happy Birthday".
"Not yet, not yet," said the Pope, who will be 77 on May 18.

Tens of thousands of Moslems and Christians earlier gave him a rousing reception on his route from Beirut airport through battle-scarred streets to the presidential palace for talks with political and religious leaders.

They threw rice and rose petals, ululated and set free white doves as the Pontiff's bulletproof "Popemobile" passed by to a welcome far more enthusiastic than the one he received a month ago on a pilgrimage to Sarajevo, Bosnia's capital.
President Elias Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, told the Pope he was "the image of hope for all the Lebanese people".
Security was heavy for the weekend visit, which was to include an big open-air mass on Sunday on the old civil war Green Line between mainly Moslem West and Christian East Beirut.
In his arrival speech, the Pope said all Lebanese should be given an equal opportunity to join in rebuilding the country.
He also made a veiled call for the withdrawal of 35,000 Syrian troops stationed in Lebanon and 2,000 Israeli troops who hold a border occupation zone in the south.
He said he had come to Lebanon to encourage its sons and daughters, "so desirous of independence and freedom" and whose national territory should be "recognised and respected by all".
Lebanese bishops at a synod at the Vatican in 1995 called bluntly for the pull-out of Syrian and Israeli forces and criticised what they saw as sectarian isolation of Christians.

The Pope at Saturday's service signed a document entitled "A New Hope for Lebanon" that concludes the synod process and will be published on Sunday. It will be watched closely for the extent to which the Pope's message echoes that of his bishops.
Many of Lebanon's Christians accuse the Beirut government of surrendering its powers of decision to Syria, while most Moslems see the departure of the Israelis as their top priority.
